name: Odoo
tagline: An integrated business suite: accounting, CRM, inventory, manufacturing, HR, ecommerce and POS sharing one database.

pricing.basis: per user per month, plus per-app on the free tier
pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Odoo is not an app, it is roughly forty apps that agree on one schema, and the agreeing is the product. An agent can absolutely generate a contacts table, an invoice table and a stock-on-hand view in an afternoon; what it cannot generate is double-entry accounting that survives an audit, country-specific tax localizations, e-invoicing formats, payroll rules, or the thousand small reconciliations between a sales order, a delivery note and a journal entry. The moment your fake ERP touches real money or real tax filings, the interesting work is legal, not technical. If you only need one slice, say a personal invoice log or a parts inventory, build the slice and skip the suite. If you need the suite, you need the suite.
coreLoopDIY: A self-hosted single-user ops tracker: contacts, products with stock levels, quotes that become invoices, and a plain cash-basis ledger you export to CSV for your accountant.
requirements: Node 20 and a machine or VPS to run it on
Willingness to do your actual accounting somewhere else
Manual data entry, since nothing syncs from your bank or store
whatYouLose: Real double-entry accounting with locked periods, audit trail and closing entries
Country tax localizations, VAT/GST reporting and certified e-invoicing formats
Every other module you did not build: purchasing, manufacturing BOMs, payroll, POS, ecommerce, field service
Thousands of third-party modules and an implementation partner ecosystem when you get stuck
Multi-user roles, approvals and the assurance that two people editing stock does not corrupt the numbers
moatNotes: The localization packs are the real asset: dozens of countries of tax logic, chart-of-accounts templates and invoice formats, maintained as the rules change.
whyPeopleStillPay: Nobody buys Odoo because the CRM is delightful. They buy it because the invoice, the delivery, the stock move and the journal entry are the same fact recorded once, and because someone else keeps the tax rules current for the country they operate in. Replacing that with a hand-rolled app means either doing your books twice or being personally liable for the bugs. Once inventory history and receivables live inside it, the switching cost is not the software, it is the years of transactions you cannot re-key.
notes: An agent can clone the forms in a weekend; it cannot clone the accounting. The moat is compliance: localized tax, chart-of-accounts and e-invoicing logic for dozens of jurisdictions, kept current by people who read tax bulletins for a living.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted, single-user small-business ops tracker. This is deliberately NOT an ERP: no double-entry accounting, no tax engine, no payroll.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript, server actions, no client-side state library
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, single file at ./data/ops.db, schema created on boot with plain SQL migrations in /migrations
- Tailwind for styling, no component library
- No auth beyond a single shared password read from .env (BASIC_PASSWORD), enforced in middleware
- No accounts, no cloud services, no telemetry, no analytics

In scope:
1. Contacts: name, type (customer/supplier), email, phone, address, notes. List + detail + edit.
2. Products: SKU, name, unit, unit price, current stock quantity.
3. Stock moves: append-only table (product, delta, reason, date). Product stock is always derived by summing moves, never stored as a mutable number.
4. Quotes and invoices: one document type with a status field (draft, sent, paid, cancelled). Line items reference products or free text, with quantity and unit price. Auto-incrementing human-readable number per year. A single flat tax rate per document, entered manually, clearly labelled in the UI as "not a tax engine".
5. Marking an invoice paid records a payment row (date, amount, method). Partial payments allowed; show outstanding balance.
6. Dashboard: outstanding receivables total, overdue invoice list, products below a per-product reorder point.
7. CSV export for contacts, invoices, payments and stock moves. Print-friendly invoice page via CSS print styles.

Out of scope, do not build: journals, chart of accounts, VAT returns, purchase orders, manufacturing, POS, ecommerce, email sending, multi-user roles, mobile app.

Deliverables: working app on npm run dev, .env.example, a seed script with three contacts and five products, and a README that says in one line that this is a bookkeeping input tool and real accounting still happens elsewhere.
